humanities_role_explanation: Historical newspaper articles supply the items, but the competence tested is generic post-OCR text correction (sequence-to-sequence / prompt-based), not disciplinary humanities competence. The paper uses an existing corpus (BLN600) rather than designing a humanities-competence benchmark.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Text-only: OCR text sequences are input and re-keyed human transcriptions are targets. Source page images are not shown to models.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Post-OCR correction of 19th century British newspaper text, framed as neural machine translation for BART and as prompt-based instruction following ('Fix the OCR errors in the provided text') for Llama 2. Error types analysed: substitution, insertion, deletion, misnamed entity, hallucination.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Scoped to a single task (post-OCR correction) on a single dataset of 19th century newspaper articles.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Llama 2 7B and 13B base models instruction-tuned with LoRA, compared with fine-tuned BART base and large.

quantitative_metrics.note: Percentage reduction in character error rate (CER), based on Levenshtein distance.

summary: The paper instruction-tunes Llama 2 (7B, 13B) with LoRA for post-OCR correction of BLN600, a parallel corpus of 19th century British newspaper articles, and compares it to fine-tuned BART. Llama 2 13B achieves a 54.51% CER reduction versus 23.30% for BART large, and Llama 2 performs well even with little training data.
key_findings: Llama 2 13B reduces CER by 54.51%, Llama 2 7B by 43.26%, BART large by 23.30% and BART base by 14.60%. BART improves significantly with more training data whereas Llama 2 is strong from the outset with 80 training samples. Substitutions and deletions are easiest to correct; insertions and heavily corrupted named entities are harder.
evaluation_unit: sequence pair (OCR segment / ground-truth segment, mostly sentences)
gold_upstream: BLN600 (Booth et al., 2024): OCR excerpts from British Library Newspapers paired with manually re-keyed human transcriptions from the source images; further production details not described in this paper.
facets_explanation: Reference texts are the manually re-keyed human transcriptions from BLN600 (Booth et al., 2024), an existing corpus prepared by colleagues. The paper segments the ground truth into sentence-level pairs and scores predictions against the single reference with CER. It does not discuss how the transcriptions were produced beyond 'high-quality manually re-keyed', nor annotator disagreement.
results_explanation: Table 3 gives the CER reduction (%): 'BART 140M 14.60', 'BART 400M 23.30', 'Llama 2 7B 43.26', 'Llama 2 13B 54.51', each the mean over five training and evaluation iterations. The metric is percentage reduction in CER (not a standard metric label), so it is recorded as 'other'. A training-set-size comparison (six subsets of 80 samples, Fig. 3) is shown only graphically, so no gap in points is given.

humanities_role.quote: Poor OCR quality continues to be a major obstacle for humanities scholars seeking to make use of digitised primary sources such as historical newspapers.

primary_evaluation_setting.quote: By instruction-tuning Llama 2 and comparing it to a fine-tuned BART on BLN600

gold_source.quote: This dataset contains OCR text sourced from British Library Newspapers along with manually re-keyed human transcriptions.

gold_beyond_stimulus.quote: mapping erroneous OCR texts to accurate reference texts

answer_multiplicity.quote: computing the Levenshtein distance between the recognised text and the reference text and dividing it by the total number of characters in the reference text
